According to Mark Gurman's latest issue of the *Power On* newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making several changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the App Store can generate.

Specific details of Apple's App Store overhaul remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," with the work primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current services SVP Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this overhaul was one of the reasons veteran employee Phil Schiller left Apple last week. Schiller stepped down as SVP of marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, with part of his responsibilities including overseeing the App Store. Schiller expressed opposition to the proposals:

Apple has many ways to improve App Store margins. For example, it could eliminate the manual app review process—in the age of automated coding, this procedure is both costly and widely questioned. Further automation of reviews might upset users, but it would undoubtedly save money.

Apple could also raise developer membership fees, currently set at US$99 per year. Given that many small developers spend US$200 a month on Codex and Claude subscriptions to build apps, Apple is in a position to raise prices without facing too much resistance. Apple could also charge subscription fees to large developers based on traffic, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

What the final outcome will be remains unknown, but I'm very much looking forward to seeing what these changes look like once they are eventually implemented.
